# Route accounting {#sec-method}

## Setting

A model processes a prompt and generates text. An intervention changes the
information available at a set of **source** positions \(S\). Its effect is measured
at a later **target** position \(t\), where that information is used. The positions
strictly between them, \(M\), include the end of the prompt and the tokens generated
so far. Every intervention in this paper is an **all-layer state edit**: the residual
stream at every layer of each source position is replaced by the corresponding
states of a *donor* prompt that differs only in the content under study. Examples
are a first line with a different rhyme, or a list in a different order. The text of
the prompt is unchanged. The outcome is a log-odds contrast at the target:

$$
R \;=\; \log \sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{\rm donor}} p(v\mid\cdot) \;-\; \log \sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{\rm orig}} p(v\mid\cdot),
$$

where \(\mathcal V_{\rm donor}\) and \(\mathcal V_{\rm orig}\) are the tokens
consistent with the donor's and the original content. Examples are the single-token
perfect rhymes of each rhyme word, the donor's and the original pick, or the donor's
and the original first digit. Effects are changes in \(R\) relative to the unedited
run; positive values move the target toward the donor.

## Emission and persistence

Generation closes a loop: the edit can change what the model writes, and the
written tokens are read back. Let \(g_0\) and \(g_1\) be the texts generated with the
edit off and on, and let \(R(i,g)\) be the outcome with the edit in state
\(i\in\{0,1\}\) and the text fixed to \(g\). Then

$$
\underbrace{R(1,g_1)-R(0,g_0)}_{\text{total}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{R(0,g_1)-R(0,g_0)}_{\text{emission}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{R(1,g_1)-R(0,g_1)}_{\text{persistence}} .
$$

**Emission** is the effect of the edited text alone: the edited words are replayed
with the edit off. **Persistence** is what the edit does when the text is held fixed.
We also report persistence with the original text, \(R(1,g_0)-R(0,g_0)\), which is
the other order of the decomposition. Where the two orders differ, we give both. For a binary mediator
such as the article *a/an*, emission factorizes exactly into the change in the
mediator policy times the leverage of the mediator on the continuation
(@sec-emission). This four-cell design is the multi-token form of the six-cell assay
used for single-token mediators (Appendix @sec-app-sixcell).

## Paths within persistence

Persistence can reach the target in two structurally different ways. The target
can read the edited source positions itself (**direct retrieval**). Alternatively,
intermediate positions read the edited source and pass it on, and the target reads
them (an **indirect path**). We separate the two by clamping states. Let \(h^{0}\) and \(h^{1}\)
be the per-layer states of the clean run and of the edited run, both with the text
fixed. Write \(R[\,S\!\leftarrow\!a,\;G\!\leftarrow\!b\,]\) for the outcome when the
source positions receive the states of run \(a\), and a group of intermediate
positions \(G\subseteq M\) receives the states of run \(b\), at every layer. All
other positions are recomputed. With \(R_0\) the clean outcome,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= R[S\!\leftarrow\!1] - R_0 &&\text{persistence,}\\
D &= R[S\!\leftarrow\!1,\;M\!\leftarrow\!0] - R_0 &&\text{direct retrieval (every intermediate position clean),}\\
T &= R[M\!\leftarrow\!1] - R_0 &&\text{indirect paths (source clean, intermediates as in the edited run),}\\
\Delta &= P - D - T &&\text{interaction (additivity gap).}
\end{aligned}
$$

Because the intermediate states are overwritten at every layer, \(D\) can reach the
target only through the target's own attention to the source. \(T\) can reach it
only through the intermediate positions. For a group \(G\) we report its
**interventional sufficiency**, \(\mathrm{Suf}(G)=R[G\!\leftarrow\!1]-R_0\): the
effect of the group alone, given its edited-run states. We also report its
**interventional necessity**,
\(\mathrm{Nec}(G)=P-\big(R[S\!\leftarrow\!1,\,G\!\leftarrow\!0]-R_0\big)\): the loss of
persistence when the group alone is reset to its clean states. By construction
\(\mathrm{Nec}(M)=P-D\). When paths combine additively, the two measures agree and the
interaction is small. Shares then partition the effect, and we write that a share
"travels by" a path. When the interaction is large, shares are not exclusive. A clean
source that contradicts an edited copy downstream makes sufficiency understate the
copy, and necessity does not. There we report both measures, the interaction, and the
Shapley value of the two-player game between the source and the group, which is
their average [@shapley1953]. The largest interactions are in Gemma 3 27B couplets
(29% of persistence with the chat prompt, 33% with the plain prompt). All quantities
are reported with item-bootstrap 95% intervals (10,000 resamples; @efron1994bootstrap). Shares are
divided by the persistence of the same run, unless another denominator is named,
which makes model families with different log-probability scales comparable.

**Path names.** We split the intermediate positions into three groups by position,
not by any hypothesis about their content, and name the indirect path through each:

- the **stored copy**: the path through the prompt positions right after the source
  line (in couplets, the comma ending line 1 and the chat template). The copy is
  written once into a fixed position of the prompt and read directly from there;
- the **late lookup**: the path through the three positions immediately before the
  target. This is the late retrieval of @hanna2026latent read in two steps: those
  positions retrieve the plan just before use, and the target reads them;
- **relay**: the path through the remaining positions of the generated text. This is
  the path monitoring is concerned with.

Throughout the paper, *direct retrieval*, *stored copy*, *late lookup*, *relay*,
*emission* and *interaction* keep these meanings and one colour each (@fig-overview A).
We say information is **looked up** when it arrives by direct retrieval, a stored copy
or the late lookup. Where a group of intermediate positions was not split into these
parts, we name the group and call its effect the indirect path through it.

## Positive control: induction {#sec-control}

A decomposition that never reports an indirect path could be blind to one. We
therefore apply route accounting where an indirect path is the established
mechanism. In a repeated sequence
\(\ldots A\,B\ldots A\), a previous-token head writes "preceded by \(A\)" into the
position of \(B\), and an induction head at the second \(A\) finds that position and
copies \(B\) [@olsson2022induction]. Information about the first \(A\) therefore
reaches the prediction through \(B\)'s position. The design is 100 random sequences
of 24 distinct common word tokens, repeated up to the second \(A\). The edit replaces
the first \(A\)'s states with those of a sequence identical except for that token.
The outcome is \(\log p(B)\) at the second \(A\). The criterion, committed before the
first result, was that the indirect path accounts for more than 80% of persistence and
direct retrieval is near zero.

The control passes cleanly in four models and partly in five (@fig-overview B;
@tbl-control).

- *Clean pass.* In Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B, direct retrieval is 1 to 3% of
  persistence, and the indirect path is 108 to 137%. Shares above 100% reflect an
  interaction: with only the downstream positions edited, the clean first \(A\)
  conflicts with the edited "preceded by" signal and suppresses \(B\) more than the
  consistent edit does.
- *Partial pass, from the same interaction.* In Gemma 3 12B and 27B, direct retrieval
  is 0.4%, but the indirect path through all intermediate positions is only 53% and
  55%. Editing
  \(B\)'s first position alone gives 145% and 156%, so the conflicting edited positions
  weaken the all-position cell.
- *Partial pass, because the model also reads the source.* The indirect path remains
  the main path
  in Qwen3-32B (89%) and in the recurrent hybrids Qwen3.5-9B and 27B (key position alone
  96% and 77%). But direct retrieval is 31%, 10% and 17%: these models also read the
  first \(A\) directly.

In every model, the indirect path is the largest path, so the method detects an
indirect path where one is the mechanism. The key position, \(B\)'s first occurrence,
lies right after the source in the prompt. Structurally this path therefore resembles
a stored copy more than relay along generated text. What the control establishes is
that route accounting detects an effect that arrives through an intermediate position.
Relay is the same kind of path through different positions. Persistence holds the
generated text fixed, so during measurement generated tokens are ordinary context
positions, and the clamp is the same operation at any position. The retrieval-dominated results in the rest of the paper are
therefore informative negatives, not a blind spot of the method.

## Models, materials and protocol {#sec-models}

We study Qwen3 1.7B to 32B, dense with full attention [@yang2025qwen3], and Gemma 3
1B to 27B, which interleaves five sliding-window layers with a 1,024-token window per
global layer [@gemma3]. Both families are used as instruction-tuned models, with base
checkpoints as checks. We also study Qwen3.5 4B, 9B and 27B, hybrids in which three of
every four layers are Gated DeltaNet recurrent layers [@qwen2026qwen35;
@yang2025gateddeltanet], and Gemma 4 31B [@gemma4] for the hidden choice. Qwen3 runs
with thinking disabled throughout, so every generated span is short: part of a line,
a sentence, or up to 2,000 tokens of filler. Models run in bfloat16. Where effects are
small, the output projection is recomputed in float32, because bfloat16 logits resolve
only about 0.125 nats. After the initial couplet split, the design, decision rule and
predictions of every experiment and extension were committed to the repository before
its first result. Later additions are dated and labelled post hoc (Appendix
@sec-app-prereg). Nulls are reported with the same prominence as effects. Model
identifiers, prompts, item construction and per-run tables are in Appendix
@sec-app-materials.
